cards.name: Clean natural correction
cards.summary: A neutral, honest fix for a flat or slightly dark photo: shadows opened, a little contrast and colour, nothing that reads as a filter.
use_for: news, documentary and event photos that must stay truthful
product and catalogue photos before layout
a first pass before any creative grade
batch-correcting a shoot to one baseline
avoid: adding, removing or moving content in a news or documentary photo: keep every change global and tonal
a photo that is already well exposed: Shadows/Highlights then only flattens it; skip that step
strong colour casts: neutralise with Temperature / Tint first and check skin and greys
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object on the photo layer: ran (the label 'photo' now names the converted layer, Layer 0), so the next adjustment sits on a smart object.

Image > Adjustments > Shadows/Highlights on the smart object: Color Correction 20, default Shadows amount. Ran. The run shows the darks opened and the photo lighter overall. Untested: other Shadows / Highlights amounts (the card's example uses 50 / 15); they travel in object params a plan cannot carry.
Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer above: Contrast +12, non-legacy. Ran without error.
Color and vibrance adjustment layer on top: Vibrance +15, Temperature and Tint 0. Ran; colours a little stronger. Untested: cast correction (Temperature / Tint left at 0).
label photo now names the result (new layer ID); history: Convert to Smart Object; active layer: Layer 0
history: Shadows/Highlights; active layer: Layer 0
history: New Brightness/Contrast Layer; active layer: Brightness/Contrast 1
history: New Color and vibrance Layer; active layer: Color and vibrance 1

verified.note: Shadows clearly opened (black point about 44 to 64, photo lighter overall) with a touch more colour and no filter look; overall it is slightly flatter than the input, since Shadows/Highlights outweighs the +12 contrast.

steps.note: Light effect (CorelDRAW's Shadows/Highlights with contrast): Shadows +45 opens the dark clothing and dim wall, Highlights -10 holds the bright areas, Contrast +20 restores the punch the lifted shadows take away. The first run used Auto Adjust, which darkened the photo, and a gamma that only undid it. Measured on the frame: the darkest 2 percent of tones rise from about 48 to 59 of 255, the mean lightness from 112 to 119, and the spread of tones stays the same.
Vibrance +15, saturation 0: a little more colour, mostly in the duller tones; nothing here reads as a filter.
ApplyBitmapEffect('SMHEffect Brightness=0,Intensity=0,Midtones=0,Shadows=45,Highlights=-10,Contrast=20')
ApplyBitmapEffect('VibranceEffect Vibrance=15,Saturation=0')

verified.note: Now a visible, honest global fix: the darkest 2% rise from 48 to 59 of 255, dark clothing from about 63 to 73, mean lightness 112 to 120, colour slightly up and tonal spread unchanged, with nothing that reads as a filter. The input's warm cast is kept (slightly stronger), not neutralised.

cards.name: Cinematic teal and orange
cards.summary: The blockbuster grade: shadows pushed toward teal, highlights and warm tones toward orange, with a little extra contrast.
use_for: film-poster and trailer-style key art
travel and lifestyle social posts
YouTube thumbnails and banners that want a movie feel
unifying photos from different cameras into one look
avoid: skin-heavy close-ups: too much orange turns skin brown; keep the gradient layer at 30-40 % opacity
news photos: a stylised grade changes how the scene reads
CorelDRAW: no scripted split toning on a colour photo (its Color Balance render failed and Tone Curve needs input); grade in Photoshop
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Gradient Map adjustment layer (script): three stops, saturated teal (0, 105, 125) at 0, a warm neutral (150, 125, 105) at 50 and orange (255, 150, 50) at 100, dither on. The step's settings can only name the stock black-to-white map, so the script builds the gradient in the descriptor (a make adjustmentLayer / gradientMapClass call). Ran.

Gradient map layer set to Color at 65 % opacity (script: blend mode and layer opacity in one call): ran. The first run used Soft Light, which left the dark tones brown. Color mode puts the map's hue and saturation on the photo's own brightness, so the darks go teal and the lights orange. Measured on the photo area of the frame: the darkest tenth of pixels averages RGB 7 / 58 / 57 (input 65 / 46 / 29) and the lightest tenth 240 / 182 / 109 (input 218 / 187 / 138).
steps.script: setMode('color'); d.activeLayer.opacity = 65;

steps.note: Color and vibrance adjustment layer: Vibrance +45, Saturation +5 (+20 / -5 in the first run, which left the Color-mode grade muted). Ran; colour is stronger, overall saturation back above the input's.

Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer: Contrast +15. Ran. The run shows teal-tinted dark areas (the dark foreground, the dark end of the grey ramp), orange-gold walls and mid-tones; the colour bars' reds and purples are muted by the grade. Untested: the teal / orange balance and layer opacity are taste; judge them on screen (manual).

The first judge's warm-brown shadows are fixed; the colour bars' reds and purples are muted by the grade, as the step note says.

manual_steps: Judge the teal / orange balance on screen: the stop colours and the layer opacity are taste, and the coloured gradient map has no render test yet.

cards.name: Warm nostalgic
cards.summary: A soft, warm, slightly faded memory look: amber cast, gentler colour, a light vignette and fine grain.
use_for: throwback and anniversary posts
family, food and travel photos with a cosy mood
festival greetings and invitation backgrounds
lifestyle brand imagery with a vintage feel
avoid: already warm indoor photos: they go muddy orange; lower the filter density or skip it
product shots where colour accuracy matters
heavy grain on images that will be shrunk for social: it turns to mush; keep Amount low
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object on the photo layer: ran (label 'photo' now names the converted Layer 0).
Filter > Lens Correction on the smart object, used for its vignette only: Vignette Amount -35, Midpoint 40, automatic geometry correction off. Ran without error; the corners darken gently.
Photo Filter adjustment layer: orange #EC8A00, Density 30, Preserve Luminosity on. Ran; the run shows a gentle amber cast.
Color and vibrance adjustment layer: Temperature +10, Vibrance -15, Saturation -5. Ran; the colours are more muted.
Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer: Brightness +5, Contrast -10. Ran; slightly lighter and softer.
Grain adjustment layer on top: Amount 25, Size 35, Roughness 55. Ran without error. Untested: how visible the grain is at 100 % or after shrinking.

verified.note: Gentle amber cast, muted colour, visibly darkened corners and fine grain over the whole frame; reads as a soft warm memory look.

steps.note: White Balance at 4000 K, tint 0 (values below 5000 K warm). Run: the page changed by 8.69 on average (0-255). An amber cast is visible.
Vibrance -15, saturation -5. Run: the page changed by 4.04 on average (0-255).

Vignette: Black, Ellipse, Offset 150, Fade 80. Offset is the size of the clear area in percent: 20 left only a small bright ellipse (a first run nearly black), 150 leaves just the corners dark; Fade 80 softens the edge.
Add Noise: Gaussian, level 20, density 40, intensity mode. Run: the page changed by 0.79 on average (0-255). The grain is not visible at the 960 px frame.

cards.name: Faded matte film
cards.summary: Lifted, matte blacks, lower contrast and softened colour with grain: the faded film-stock look of lifestyle and editorial feeds.
use_for: lifestyle, fashion and café photography
moody social feeds and story backgrounds
quote cards and text-over-photo layouts (lifted blacks keep type readable)
softening harsh phone photos
avoid: prints on uncoated paper: lifted blacks look washed out; lift less
low-light photos with noise: the lifted shadows reveal it; denoise first
the classic route is a Curves layer with the black point raised, but Curves rendered as a no-op in the harness (untested), so this recipe uses a fill layer in Lighten instead
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > New Fill Layer > Solid Color (script): a solid #5C5C5C fill layer on top of the Background (the settings-free route carries the probe's orange, so the colour comes from the script). The first run's #262626 was darker than the photo's own shadows, so it changed almost nothing. Ran.

Fill layer set to Lighten at 80 % opacity (script: blend mode and layer opacity in one call): ran. Every tone darker than the fill is lifted toward it, so the blacks go flat dark grey; the 80 % opacity keeps a little of the original darks' texture. Measured on the photo area of the frame: the 10th-percentile luma rises from 54 to 89 and the darkest tenth of pixels averages RGB 90 / 85 / 80 (input 65 / 46 / 29). The near-black strip at the bottom of the plate and the ramp's black end turn grey too.
steps.script: setMode('lighten'); d.activeLayer.opacity = 80;

steps.note: Color and vibrance adjustment layer: Temperature +5, Vibrance -20, Saturation -10. Ran; colours softer (mean saturation about half the input's by the end of the stack).
Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer: Brightness +3, Contrast -12. Ran without error.

Grain adjustment layer on top: Amount 30, Size 40, Roughness 60. Ran without error. The run shows a fine grain over the picture; untested at 100 % zoom. Lifted shadows reveal noise, so denoise first on noisy photos.

verified.note: Blacks lift to a flat warm grey (darkest tenth RGB 90/85/80, minimum luma 71 against about 1 in the input), contrast drops (luma spread 46 to 35), saturation halves (0.50 to 0.25) and a fine grain shows at 1:1. The first judge's complaint, a lift that sat below the photo's own shadows, is fixed.

steps.note: Vibrance -25, saturation -12 on the photo: softened, slightly faded colour.
Light effect on the photo: contrast -14, the recipe's lower contrast.
Add Noise on the photo: Gaussian, level 40, density 70, intensity mode: a visible film grain in the lighter tones (it is flattened where the matte layer below lifts the darkest tones).

steps.script:
m = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
m.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#333333"))
m.Outline.SetNoOutline()
m.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(0)
m.Transparency.MergeMode = 11
result = m
steps.note: Matte blacks (script): a page-size rectangle filled dark grey (#333333) above the photo with Transparency.MergeMode = If Lighter (11), the recipe's fill layer in Lighten: every tone darker than the grey is lifted to it, so the blacks become a flat dark grey (the strip at the bottom of the plate shows it). The first run used only a gamma and the black point stayed at 0. CorelDRAW's Levels and Tone Curve have no working script route here.
ApplyBitmapEffect('VibranceEffect Vibrance=-25,Saturation=-12')
ApplyBitmapEffect('SMHEffect Brightness=0,Intensity=0,Highlights=0,Shadows=0,Midtones=0,Contrast=-14')
ApplyBitmapEffect('AddNoiseEffect NoiseMode=0,Level=40,Density=70,ColorMode=0')
script ran

verified.note: Fixed: the black point now sits at a flat dark grey (minimum 2 to 51 of 255), contrast is lower (tonal spread 46 to 41), colour is softened (chroma 68 to 45) and a fine grain is visible (fine detail about 3.5 times the input). Reads as a pale, matte, faded film look, if a gentle one.

manual_steps: CorelDRAW: for truly flat blacks lay a dark-grey rectangle over the photo and set its transparency merge mode to If Lighter on the Transparency tool's property bar (PGD has no scripted card for that merge mode).
cards.note: Photoshop plan: every visual step is render-verified; CorelDRAW only approximates matte blacks with a gamma lift.

cards.name: High-contrast black and white
cards.summary: A punchy monochrome with deep blacks, bright whites and crisp midtone detail, colour channels mixed for drama.
use_for: documentary and street-photo treatments
poster and editorial portraits
making mixed-colour photos sit together in a layout
a base for duotone or spot-colour printing
avoid: a flat grey result from plain desaturation: use the channel mix, not Desaturate
skies and smooth skin at high Clarity: they get gritty; keep Clarity under 30
Illustrator: Convert to Grayscale there changes vector fill and stroke colours, not placed photos; convert the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW

steps.note: Black & White adjustment layer: Reds 60, Yellows 90, Greens 40 (the key 'grain' is the green slider), Cyans 50, Blues 0, Magentas 70, no tint. Ran; the run shows a monochrome picture with the red areas light and the blue-toned areas dark.
Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer: Contrast +40, non-legacy. Ran; deeper darks and brighter lights.
Clarity and dehaze adjustment layer: Clarity 25, Dehaze 10 (kept moderate, under the Clarity 30 the recipe warns about). Ran without error.

cards.name: Two-colour duotone poster

brand hero images in two brand colours
social carousels with a consistent colour identity
covers where a busy photo must sit behind type
avoid: two colours of similar lightness: the image loses all depth; pick one dark and one light colour
real two-ink print jobs: build a true Duotone (Photoshop Image > Mode > Duotone, CorelDRAW Bitmaps > Mode > Duotone) with the printer's inks

cards.name: Cross-processed colour
cards.summary: The look of slide film developed in the wrong chemistry: blue-shifted shadows, yellow-green highlights, high saturation and contrast.
use_for: fashion and music editorial
retro 90s and lo-fi social posts
bold nightlife and festival flyers
avoid: skin-critical portraits: the green highlights make skin sickly; mask the face area out of the gradient layer
corporate or news imagery
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Gradient Map adjustment layer (script): three stops, deep blue (20, 50, 220) at 0, a neutral (135, 130, 120) at 50 and yellow-green (160, 240, 50) at 100, dither on. The step's settings can only name the stock black-to-white map, so the script builds the gradient in the descriptor (a make adjustmentLayer / gradientMapClass call). Ran.

Gradient map layer set to Color at 55 % opacity (script: blend mode and layer opacity in one call): ran. The first run used Soft Light, which left the darks brown and the lights plain yellow. Color mode puts the map's hue and saturation on the photo's own brightness. Measured on the photo area of the frame: the darkest tenth of pixels averages RGB 29 / 28 / 102 (input 65 / 46 / 29: now blue) and the lightest tenth 205 / 210 / 67 (input 218 / 187 / 138: yellow with a green lean).
steps.script: setMode('color'); d.activeLayer.opacity = 55;

steps.note: Color and vibrance adjustment layer: Tint 0, Vibrance +35, Saturation +15 (Tint -10, +30, +10 in the first run). Ran; stronger colour, overall saturation above the input's.

cards.name: Single-colour accent pop

social posts where one element must lead the eye
editorial covers with a single colour accent
advertising visuals built around one signature colour

colour families that blend into skin (reds, oranges): skin may keep colour; tighten the fuzziness or mask by hand

cards.name: Night-time cool grade
cards.summary: A darker, blue, slightly desaturated grade that reads as dusk or night, for moody or cinematic scenes.
use_for: moody cinematic posters
turning a dull daylight shot into a dusk scene
tech, security or mystery themed visuals
backgrounds for neon or glowing type
avoid: bright midday photos with hard shadows: they look like underexposed day, not night; add a vignette and keep lights glowing
photos with skin in the foreground: cool grades turn skin grey; mask it
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Exposure adjustment layer: Exposure -0.6, Offset 0, Gamma 1.0 (-0.8, -0.02, 0.9 in the first run, whose negative offset crushed the darkest tones to a reddish black). Ran; the photo area's average brightness falls to about two thirds of the input's.

Color Balance adjustment layer (script, new step): Shadows Red -5 / Blue +30, Midtones Red -20 / Blue +30, Highlights Red -5 / Blue +10, Preserve Luminosity on. The first run had no step that blued the midtones, so they landed on neutral grey. Ran.
Photo Filter adjustment layer: blue #006DFF, Density 12 (20 in the first run), Preserve Luminosity on. Ran; a little extra blue on top of the Color Balance.

Color and vibrance adjustment layer (moved after the blue push): Temperature -35, Vibrance -5, Saturation -12. Ran; keeps the palette slightly muted. Measured on the photo area of the frame: the darkest tenth of pixels averages RGB 9 / 10 / 56 (blue-black; input 65 / 46 / 29), the middle tones 61 / 72 / 116 (blue; input 138 / 106 / 67) and the lightest tenth 141 / 157 / 194. A heavier desaturation here (-25 / -25) removed the blue again; mean saturation ends slightly above the input's because of the blue cast.

Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer: Contrast +10. Ran. The run shows a darker, blue picture that reads as dusk. Untested: a vignette and glowing lights, which the recipe suggests for daytime photos.

verified.note: About a third darker (mean luma 113 to 76) and blue through the whole range: darkest tenth RGB 9/10/56, midtones about 57/72/114, lightest tenth 141/157/195, with colour intensity (mean max-min chroma) down from 68 to 58. The first judge's grey midtones and reddish crushed blacks are fixed; it reads as dusk rather than deep night.

steps.note: Gamma 0.55 through the object model (Shape.ApplyEffectGamma, which the runner now picks for Gamma): below 1 darkens the midtones, about a stop and a half darker, as the recipe's exposure step.
Vibrance -10, saturation -5, as in the recipe: the colours are muted.
Light effect: contrast +10, as in the recipe's Brightness/Contrast layer.

steps.script:
cool = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
cool.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#8FB0FF"))
cool.Outline.SetNoOutline()
cool.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(0)
cool.Transparency.MergeMode = 9
lift = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
lift.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#101E48"))
lift.Outline.SetNoOutline()
lift.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(0)
lift.Transparency.MergeMode = 7
result = cool
steps.note: Cool grade (script): two page-size rectangles above the photo as the colour layers. A pale blue (#8FB0FF) in Multiply mode (Transparency.MergeMode 9) removes red and green, the blue 'filter'; a deep blue (#101E48) in Add mode (7) lifts the shadows toward blue. They stand in for the recipe's blue Photo Filter layer, because CorelDRAW's Photo Filter ignored the colour it was given in this harness (it always warmed the picture) and Color Balance / Levels have no working script route. The photo now reads blue-grey and dim, like dusk.
Shape.ApplyEffectGamma(0.55,) (the gallery's object-model route for this effect)
ApplyBitmapEffect('VibranceEffect Vibrance=-10,Saturation=-5')
ApplyBitmapEffect('SMHEffect Brightness=0,Intensity=0,Highlights=0,Shadows=0,Midtones=0,Contrast=10')
script ran

verified.note: Fixed: the photo itself now turns blue and dim (mean lightness 112 to 71, blue minus red from -68 to +36; the cream wall becomes slate blue, the clothing navy, the lamps cool white) with muted colour, reading as dusk. The navy lift raises the shadows (darkest 2% at 37), so it is a little hazy and lower in contrast than the recipe's +10.

cards.name: Bleach bypass
cards.summary: Silver-retention film look: harsh contrast, crushed and gritty midtones, colour drained to about half, for gritty war, sport or thriller visuals.
use_for: gritty sport, action and thriller posters
industrial and urban photography
dramatic advertising key art
avoid: soft beauty, food and product photography: it makes everything harsh
already high-contrast photos: shadows block up; lower the overlay opacity
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Black & White adjustment layer above the photo: Reds 40, Yellows 60, Greens 40, Cyans 60, Blues 20, Magentas 80. Ran.
Black & White layer set to Overlay at 60 % opacity (script: blend mode and layer opacity in one call): ran. The run shows more contrast and less colour than the original.
steps.script: setMode('overlay'); d.activeLayer.opacity = 60;

steps.note: Color and vibrance adjustment layer: Vibrance -4, Saturation -16 (Saturation -15 alone left about 85 % of the colour in the first run). Ran; together with the Overlay layer the photo area's mean saturation (HSV) falls from 0.50 to 0.25, about half.

Color Balance adjustment layer (script, new step): Midtones Red -4 / Blue +8, Highlights Red -10 / Blue +28, Preserve Luminosity on: takes the warm cast out of the lights. The first run's highlights stayed warm cream. Ran; the lightest tenth of pixels averages RGB 222 / 213 / 208 (input 218 / 187 / 138), a near-neutral silvery white.

Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer: Contrast +15 (+10 in the first run). Ran. The run is harsher and grittier than the plain photo: the 10th and 90th percentile luma move from 54 / 170 to 32 / 192. Untested: lowering the overlay opacity on already high-contrast photos.

Both of the first judge's complaints, the mild desaturation and the cream highlights, are fixed.

Desaturate on the copy: the picture becomes grey tones.
Light effect on the copy: contrast +35, so the overlay is harsh.
Add Noise on the copy: a little grit in the midtones.

s.Transparency.MergeMode = 29

steps.note: Overlay at 60 percent (script): uniform transparency 40 and Transparency.MergeMode = Overlay (29) on the grey copy, as the recipe's Black & White layer in Overlay at 60 percent. Measured on the frame: the spread of tones rises from 46 to 64 and the colour strength falls from 68 to 29 (under half).
Vibrance -30, saturation -35 on the photo underneath: more colour drained (the recipe's saturation -15 step, stronger, because the grey overlay already carries the contrast).

verified.note: Fixed: harsh contrast (tonal spread 46 to 64, 2-98% range 48-208 to 24-228), crushed darks, colour drained to about 42% (chroma 68 to 29), bright near-neutral highlights and a fine grit. A slight warm residue of the input stays in the highlights, but it reads as bleach bypass.

cards.note: Photoshop plan is the real overlay technique (render-verified parts); the CorelDRAW plan approximates it with desaturation and a gamma curve.

cards.name: Sepia vintage print
cards.summary: A warm brown-toned monochrome with softened contrast, vignette and grain, like an old photographic print.
use_for: heritage, history and anniversary visuals
archival-style photo pages
invitations and certificates with an old-photo feel
avoid: presenting a new photo as a historical document
low-resolution photos: grain and vignette exaggerate the softness
Illustrator: it has no photo grading; grade the photo in Photoshop or CorelDRAW and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object on the photo layer: ran (label 'photo' now names the converted Layer 0).
Filter > Lens Correction on the smart object, used for its vignette: Vignette Amount -50, Midpoint 35, geometry correction off. Ran; the corners darken.

Hue/Saturation adjustment layer with Colorize on (script): Hue 38, Saturation 28, Lightness 0 in the adjustment list. At the plan route's default hue the first run was a rose-pink monotone, not a sepia; hue 38 gives a brown. Ran.
Photo Filter adjustment layer: orange #EC8A00, Density 20, Preserve Luminosity on. Ran; the brown shifts a little warmer.
Brightness/Contrast adjustment layer: Contrast -10. Ran; softer, like an old print.
Grain adjustment layer on top: Amount 30, Size 45, Roughness 60. Ran without error. Untested: grain visibility at 100 %, and that a low-resolution photo exaggerates grain and vignette.

Add Noise: Gaussian, level 25, density 45, intensity mode. Run: the page changed by 1.04 on average (0-255). The vignette is visible; the grain is not at the 960 px frame.
